classification.difficultyReason: Combine three compass angle-bisection constructions and a perpendicular construction to locate and draw a circle touching all three sides. The catalogue has no compass-construction skill.

answer.short: Sample triangle: see the shared construction.
answer.worked: Draw a large triangle with one interior angle greater than $90^\circ$. The shared sample has its obtuse angle at $C$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Use a ruler and compasses to construct the bisector of each vertex angle.

answer.short: The three constructed angle bisectors meet at one point, $I$.
answer.worked: At each vertex, draw an arc cutting both sides. From its two intersection points, draw equal-radius arcs meeting inside the angle. Join the vertex to that intersection. Repeat at the other two vertices, retaining the construction arcs. The three bisectors meet at $I$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: These bisectors should be concurrent. Construct the circle with centre at this point that just touches each of the three sides.

answer.short: Draw the circle with centre $I$ and radius equal to the perpendicular distance from $I$ to a side.
answer.worked: Construct a perpendicular from $I$ to a side, meeting it at $T$, using the taught perpendicular construction. Set the compasses to $IT$ and draw a circle centred at $I$. A point on an angle bisector is equally distant from its two arms: folding along the bisector matches the arms and their perpendicular distances. Therefore $I$ has the same perpendicular distance from all three sides, so the circle touches each side.

spec.description: Authored sample final construction, not a source-supplied figure. An obtuse triangle contains its three concurrent internal angle bisectors and its incircle. The perpendicular radius to the horizontal side is shown.
spec.mathematics: A=(0,0), B=(8,0), C=(2,2) gives an obtuse angle at C. The incenter is calculated by side-length weights; the radius is twice the triangle area divided by its perimeter. Each bisector endpoint uses the angle-bisector ratio.
